extracted.intended_audience: writers, critics, and students of comic literature
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on recognising, composing, and critiquing literary Comedy — its intellectual idea, character-drawing, social conditions, tone, and distinctions from satire, irony, and humour. Focus is on stage/novelistic comic art and comic perception in readers/audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy's life is in the idea
rubrics_metrics.description: The life of the comedy is in the idea; plots may be thin but the Comic flourishes when guided by a central idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even where 'the fable is thin' the play/essay can succeed if it embodies a strong Comic idea. 'To love Comedy you must know the real world... and be receptive of the idea of Comedy.' Examples: Misanthrope's strength lies in its idea rather than elaborate plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Idealised yet realistic character-painting
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters should be realistically observed but painted with 'spiritual strength'—idealized types founded on real life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Produce vivid characters (e.g., Celimene, Alceste, Micio, Sganarelle) whose types endure; the foundation must be real but the treatment can be uplifting or spiritual to create lasting comic types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Active comic spirit vs passive comic figures
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish active comic agents (who drive wit and intrigue) from passively comic figures; the active spirit often carries the humour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Celimene is 'the active spirit' while Alceste is 'only passively comic.' Favor characters who create comic situations rather than merely react to them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge of the real world and human nature
rubrics_metrics.description: To create or appreciate pure Comedy one must 'know the real world, and know men and women well enough not to expect too much of them.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comic perception needs realistic social observation; writers should avoid unrealistic expectations of human behaviour and instead work from accurate social/human detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social conditions necessary for Comedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy flourishes where there is some social equality and freedom (notably of women); where sexes are rigidly separated or women hidden, Comedy is stifled or devolves into grossness or melodrama.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay argues that 'where the veil is over women's faces, you cannot have society' and therefore comic dialogue reflecting life is absent. When constructing comic worlds, ensure a social texture that allows open intercourse and repartee.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic perception must avoid contempt and anger
rubrics_metrics.description: Comic intelligence does not entertain contempt; disdain and anger blunt the Comic and are signs of its absence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid a disdainful or angrily superior voice toward foolish characters. The Comic should perceive folly without shutting the mind ('Contempt is a sentiment that cannot be entertained by comic intelligence').

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic as corrective and proactive (attack folly early)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Comic is the proper instrument to expose and extinguish Folly early and lightly rather than waiting for heavy-handed scientific or editorial assaults.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rather than a slow defensive campaign against folly, apply Comic perception to catch and neutralize delusions before they solidify. The Comic should be used as a nimble corrective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish comic from satire, irony, and humour
rubrics_metrics.description: The Comic is a governing perceptive spirit distinct from satire (which wounds), irony (which stings ambiguously), and humour (which comforts and pities).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the appropriate mode: if you 'sting him under a semi-caress' you're using irony; to 'laugh all round him' with pity is humour; to expose with keener perception without malice is the Comic. The author gives examples and contrasts (Fielding, Jonathan Wild, Parson Adams).

rubrics_metrics.name: Capacity to detect ridicule without losing affection
rubrics_metrics.description: A mark of comic sensibility is the ability to 'detect the ridicule of them you love, without loving them less' and to see oneself as somewhat ridiculous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate self-recognition and affectionate teasing in comic depiction; this avoids slipping into satiric cruelty when showing characters' foibles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language and style: refined translucency
rubrics_metrics.description: High Comedy often uses refined, translucent language—'amenity that is like Elysian speech'—rather than coarse or overwrought diction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model language on Terence, Moliere, Shakespeare: graceful, equable speech that carries comic feeling. Avoid over-polished or artificially florid prose that obscures the Comic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure audience belief in characters' delusion without making them simpletons
rubrics_metrics.description: When a character is evidently duped, craft the scene so the audience accepts that the character is sincerely deceived without being made an absolute fool.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use comic sympathy and small touches (Orgon's 'Le pauvre homme!' example) to make the audience share the character's prepossession. Comic devices should create empathy for the deluded figure, not mere mockery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid blunting comic perception with cheap devices
rubrics_metrics.description: Overuse of punning, humouristic phrases, and polysyllabic 'playful' diction dulls the Comic sensibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not substitute flashy verbal tricks for true comic insight; 'the sense of the Comic is much blunted by habits of punning and of using humouristic phrase.' Use wit purposefully, not as filler.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect national/genre comic traditions and adapt tone
rubrics_metrics.description: Different literatures have distinct comic tendencies (French polish, Spanish sharp outline, German grotesque, Italian earthy), which shape what will read/perform as Comic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When drawing on or imitating national styles, be mindful of their strengths and limits (e.g., Spanish quick movement but skeletal outlines; German grotesque not communal laughter). Choose tone appropriate to cultural conventions and audience expectation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic requires cultivation of the audience's wit
rubrics_metrics.description: The Comic 'addresses the wits for laughter' and audiences may need training to respond; the Comic is not the same as popular jokery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers should aim at sharpening the readers' or spectators' perception: sustained Comic art expects an attentive, discerning audience rather than instant gag-laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of political Comic is powerful but risky
rubrics_metrics.description: Political comedy (à la Aristophanes) can be a forceful corrective of public folly but may provoke suppression or consequences if too sharp.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that political satire/Comedy can lead to censorship or legal/political blowback; weigh the public value against potential cost (historical example: Aristophanes' penalties).
